topic: Status quo of hospital data: quality, fragmentation, documentation burden, search effort, manual abstraction
summary: Hospital records are large and repetitive, and structured fields capture only part of what the notes say. The popular 80% figure has no traceable measurement; a large Dutch study found a structured match for only 13% of the concepts in free text. German surveys report about 3 hours of documentation per day, while direct observation finds about 1.5 hours plus considerable time for searching and reading. Existing data is error-prone before any AI: half of the note text at one US system is copied, codes miss two thirds of severe sepsis cases in ten German hospitals, and manual chart abstraction has a pooled error rate of 6.6%. The national patient record is still mostly a PDF/A collection in late 2026, and more forms cost clinician time without guaranteeing trust.

findings.claim: The popular figure that 80% of health data is unstructured has no traceable measurement behind it.
findings.detail: A medical editorial that states it (Kong 2019, Healthc Inform Res, PMC6372467) cites a 2015 HIT Consultant article. That article was sponsored by a vendor (SyTrue), names only 'cross-industry consensus' and speaks of all data, not medical data. A 2025 JMIR study also says the claim is grounded in business-related data. The general 80% claim is attributed to 1998 reports (Merrill Lynch, or Coopers & Lybrand); Mancini (CMSWire 2018) found no copy of the latter in the AIIM archives.
findings.quote: approximately 80 percent of all data remains unstructured
findings.source: HIT Consultant, Why Unstructured Data Holds the Key to Intelligent Healthcare Systems (sponsored); cited by Kong HJ, Healthc Inform Res 2019;25(1):1-2; see also Mancini, CMSWire 2018
findings.talk_use: Opening hook: follow the citation chain of the 80% number live, it ends nowhere; then show a measured number.

findings.claim: In 1.8 million Dutch GP records, only 13% of the clinical concepts found in free text had a similar structured counterpart.
findings.detail: IPCI database, Jan 2021 to Jan 2024; concepts extracted from notes by an NLP pipeline and matched by embeddings (cosine threshold 0.65). Per visit the share was 7%. In the other direction, 42% (records) and 25% (visits) of structured concepts had a match in text. Primary care, threshold-dependent, extraction errors possible.
findings.number: 13% of free-text concepts have a structured match (7% per visit)
findings.source: Using Structured Codes and Free-Text Notes to Measure Information Complementarity in Electronic Health Records, J Med Internet Res 2025;27:e66910
findings.talk_use: Replacement for the 80% slide: two circles, text and codes, with little overlap.

findings.claim: At a US academic centre, about 92 to 95% of the MedDRA terms positively mentioned in the notes of an encounter were not coded in that encounter.
findings.detail: 15,000 randomly sampled encounters (ambulatory, emergency, inpatient), 119,492 notes, MetaMap NLP versus ICD-10-CM codes, 2010 to 2023. In reverse, 40 to 50% of coded terms were not positively mentioned in the notes. Single site, no full chart review of NLP precision, inpatient stays up to 3 days.
findings.number: 92-95% of terms only in text; 40-50% of coded terms not positively mentioned in text
findings.quote: the majority of MedDRA concepts recognized in each encounter were only mentioned in text
findings.source: Smith JC et al., Characterization and comparison of structured and unstructured electronic health record data mapped to MedDRA, JAMIA Open 2026;9(2):ooag025
findings.talk_use: 2026 hospital evidence that codes miss most of what notes say, with the honest reverse finding.

findings.claim: German hospitals estimate that a physician spends 3.0 hours and a nurse 2.8 hours per working day on documentation and proof obligations.
findings.detail: DKI flash survey for the German Hospital Federation, 18 to 24 Sept 2025, 400 hospitals. Hospitals gave a lump-sum estimate per full-time post; physician quartiles 2.0 and 3.5 h. 88% report an increase in 12 months (2024: 2.9 and 2.6 h). Redundant entry because of missing IT support and interfaces is named as a driver. The commissioner has a political interest.
findings.quote: viele mehrfache und redundante Erfassungen aufgrund von fehlender IT-Unterstützung, mangelnden Schnittstellen
findings.source: Blum K, Ludwig K, Bürokratiebelastung im Krankenhaus, Blitzumfrage September 2025, Deutsches Krankenhausinstitut
findings.talk_use: Headline number for Germany, labelled as an estimate by hospitals and shown next to the observed value.

findings.claim: In the Marburger Bund survey 2024, 52% of employed physicians say data is frequently entered more than once and 65% are dissatisfied with their IT.
findings.detail: Online survey of 9,649 employed physicians, 27 Sept to 27 Oct 2024. Administrative and organisational tasks average about 3 hours per day by self-report. Survey by the physicians' union.
findings.number: 52% frequent multiple entry; 65% dissatisfied with IT
findings.source: Marburger Bund, MB-Monitor 2024, reported by Deutsches Ärzteblatt (aerztestellen)
findings.talk_use: The audience will recognise this: the same fact is typed several times.

findings.claim: When physicians in a German hospital were observed directly, documentation took 93 minutes per day (19.4%), about half of the surveyed 3 hours.
findings.detail: 9 physicians (internal medicine, surgery, anaesthesia/ICU), 216 observed hours, 5-minute intervals, one regional hospital. Internists reached 120 min (25%). Discharge letters were 32% and paper files 21% of documentation time. Pilot study; overtime and on-call excluded; narrower definition than in the surveys.
findings.source: Schröder G et al., Dtsch Med Wochenschr 2024;149(16):e67-e75, doi:10.1055/a-2335-6340
findings.talk_use: Q&A shield: the 3-hour figure is an estimate, the observed figure is lower, the burden is still large.

findings.claim: In a German university hospital, physicians spent 37% of observed time with the health record: 20.5% writing, 9.0% searching and 7.7% reading.
findings.detail: Leipzig, 13 physicians observed for 2,205 minutes, 19 interviewed, six departments. Main system SAP i.s.h.med plus COPRA in ICU and emergency, not ORBIS. Complaints: information spread over systems and tabs, repeated documentation, paper CT orders. 9% of an 8-hour day would be about 43 min (own arithmetic). Small, one site.
findings.quote: use of multiple HIT systems with limited integration
findings.source: de Hoop T, Neumuth T, Evaluating Electronic Health Record Limitations and Time Expenditure in a German Medical Center, Appl Clin Inform 2021;12(5):1082-1090
findings.talk_use: Best German source for search effort: more time goes into searching than into reading what was found.

findings.claim: In US outpatient log data, chart review was the largest EHR activity: 33% of about 16 minutes per encounter, more than documentation (24%).
findings.detail: Cerner log files 2018, about 100 million encounters, 155,000 physicians, 417 health systems. Ambulatory adult non-surgical practices, one vendor, variation by health system not analysed.
findings.source: Overhage JM, McCallie D, Physician Time Spent Using the EHR During Outpatient Encounters, Ann Intern Med 2020
findings.talk_use: Reading the record costs more time than writing it, so overview and search matter as much as dictation tools.

findings.claim: At a US emergency department, the median number of available notes per visit rose from 5 (2006) to 359 (2022), and in 2022 about one in five visits had a chart longer than Moby Dick.
findings.detail: UW Health, 730,968 ED visits, 293,559 patients, 132.6 million notes. 19.12% of encounters (Jan 2022 to Jan 2023) exceeded 206,052 words; median 98,308 tokens in 2022. Part of the growth is the start of the electronic record. Counted per encounter; outside records not included.
findings.number: 5 to 359 median notes; 19.12% of visits over 206,052 words
findings.quote: The task of reviewing these notes has become commensurately more difficult.
findings.source: Patterson et al., Call me Dr Ishmael: trends in EHR notes available at emergency department visits and admissions, JAMIA Open 2024;7(2):ooae039
findings.talk_use: Strong visual: book cover plus two numbers. Say 'visits', not 'patients'.

findings.claim: In 104 million notes of one US health system, 50.1% of all words were exact copies of earlier text about the same patient.
findings.detail: Penn Medicine 2015 to 2020, 1.96 million patients, 33 billion words; duplication rose from 33.0% (2015) to 54.2% (2020); 54.1% of it came from the same author. Exact 10-word matches only, so paraphrase is missed and templates are included. Median record 4,285 words, so most records are short. A second study (Rule et al., JAMA Netw Open 2021, PMC8290305, abstract) found only 29.4% directly typed text in 2018 outpatient notes.
findings.quote: duplication is a rational response of clinicians attempting to manage information
findings.source: Steinkamp J, Kantrowitz JJ, Airan-Javia S, Prevalence and Sources of Duplicate Information in the EMR, JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(9):e2233348
findings.talk_use: Copying is a system problem, not laziness; a source link should lead to the first mention, because copies are no independent evidence.

findings.claim: Of patients who read their outpatient notes, 21% reported a mistake, and 42% of those called it serious.
findings.detail: 22,889 note readers at three US health systems; 4,830 reported a mistake, 2,043 of them serious. Among very serious errors: diagnosis 27.5%, history 23.9%, medication or allergy 14.0%. Response rate 21.7%; reports not verified against the record.
findings.number: 21.1% found a mistake; 42.3% of those serious
findings.source: Bell SK et al., Frequency and Types of Patient-Reported Errors in EHR Ambulatory Care Notes, JAMA Netw Open 2020;3(6):e205867
findings.talk_use: Trust in existing records is limited before any AI is involved.

findings.claim: In ten German hospitals, only about a third of chart-confirmed severe sepsis cases carried a sepsis code, and only half were named as sepsis in the chart.
findings.detail: 10,334 chart reviews, 8 university and 2 teaching hospitals, 2015 to 2017. Coding sensitivity 34.4% (10.7 to 58.5% between hospitals), PPV 83.3%; hospital mortality by codes and by charts hardly correlated (r = 0.09). Follow-up analysis (Thomas-Rüddel 2025, PMC12864231): 56.2% coded when named, 5.5% when not named. Convenience sample, coding rules before 2020.
findings.quote: Due to the under-coding of sepsis in IAHD, previous epidemiological studies underestimated the burden of sepsis in Germany.
findings.source: Schwarzkopf D et al., Understanding the biases to sepsis surveillance and quality assurance caused by inaccurate coding in administrative health data, Infection 2023;52(2):413-427
findings.talk_use: Structured does not mean true. Also a limit for text extraction: what nobody wrote down can only be inferred from findings.

findings.claim: In Q2 2026, about half of the audited German inpatient bills were reduced: 50.5% nationwide and 53.0% at UKM.
findings.detail: Own aggregation of the official GKV file: 1,604 hospital rows, 575,324 completed audits, 284,598 not reducible. UKM row: 937 completed audits, 440 not reducible (46.96%), audit rate 9.67%. Audits are selected, not random, and about 60% concern length of stay or need for admission (GKV authors, f&w 5/2026), so this is not a coding error rate.
findings.source: GKV-Spitzenverband, Statistikdaten nach § 275c Abs. 4 SGB V, 2. Quartal 2026 (own calculation)
findings.talk_use: Q&A only: even money-relevant structured data is disputed in every second audited case. Showing the UKM value in public is a decision for the speaker.

findings.claim: Across ten health systems in three countries, on average 78% of patients with laboratory evidence of diabetes had diabetes on their problem list.
findings.detail: US, UK and Argentina; range 60.2 to 99.4%; criterion HbA1c of 7.0% or more. One disease, purposive sample, false positives not detectable.
findings.quote: Problem list completeness varies substantially across healthcare facilities.
findings.source: Wright A et al., Problem list completeness in electronic health records, Int J Med Inform 2015
findings.talk_use: Structured lists are incomplete even for an easy disease, but 99% is possible with culture and incentives.

findings.claim: At hospital admission, 27 to 54% of patients had at least one error in their medication history in the studies that separated errors from intended changes.
findings.detail: Systematic review, 22 studies, 3,755 patients, searched to April 2005; 5 studies (n=545) made the distinction. 11 to 59% of errors were judged clinically important. Old, heterogeneous, mostly before electronic records.
findings.source: Tam VC et al., Frequency, type and clinical importance of medication history errors at admission to hospital, CMAJ 2005;173(5):510
findings.talk_use: Supports the question 'last dose change?': the list in the system is often not the truth.

findings.claim: Manual abstraction from medical records has a pooled error rate of 6.6%, compared with 0.29% for single and 0.14% for double data entry.
findings.detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 93 papers published 1978 to 2008; mostly uncontrolled, definitions vary. The step from record to form is the weak point, not typing. With a quality control framework (training, checks), one study reached 1.04 to 2.57% (Garza 2024, BMC Med Res Methodol, abstract).
findings.source: Garza MY et al., Error rates of data processing methods in clinical research, Int J Med Inform 2025, doi:10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2024.105749 (preprint full text and published abstract read; same numbers)
findings.talk_use: Human baseline for doctoral candidates: roughly 1 in 15 hand-extracted fields is wrong; the fair comparison for an LLM is this, not perfection.

findings.claim: For a 251-patient retrospective cohort in Erlangen, manual collection took 668 hours; a data warehouse query took about 35 hours and was slightly more accurate on comparable items (93.9% vs 91.2%).
findings.detail: Meningioma radiotherapy; 637 of the 668 h were a scientific assistant. Only nine data elements could be compared. Histology, tumour site, cause of death and others stayed manual (about 25 h extra for physicist and physician). The warehouse missed half of the deaths because they happened elsewhere. 2017, one site.
findings.number: 668 h vs about 35 h; 91.2% vs 93.9% correct
findings.quote: Seven (50.0% of all deceased) patients were overlooked by the DWH report.
findings.source: Rutzner S et al., Front Oncol 2017;7:16, doi:10.3389/fonc.2017.00016
findings.talk_use: Best German slide for doctoral candidates: about 2.7 hours per patient by hand. Much of what stayed manual was free-text or image content.

findings.claim: In 2024, 56% of German hospitals were still at indicative EMRAM stage 0 (2021: 68.6%), with a mean DigitalRadar score of 42.4 of 100.
findings.detail: Second national measurement, 1,592 hospitals, self-assessment. Stage 1: 35.9%, stage 2: 3.3%. University sites average 52.9. All criteria of a stage must be met; the indicator covers about 65% of EMRAM 2018 criteria and is no certification.
findings.quote: Bis t2 sank der Anteil der Krankenhäuser in Stufe 0 von 68,6 % auf 56 %
findings.source: DigitalRadar, Zwischenbericht 2025: Ergebnisse der zweiten nationalen Reifegradmessung deutscher Krankenhäuser, BMG
findings.talk_use: German starting point in one line; add that university hospitals are above average.

findings.claim: As of October 2026, nearly all documents that hospitals must upload to the national patient record (ePA) are unstructured PDF/A files, and search beyond metadata comes in 2027 at the earliest.
findings.detail: DKG implementation guide, version 2.4, 8 Oct 2026; the medication list is structured since ePA 3.0, structured laboratory data is planned for version 27, structured discharge letters later. KBV page: full-text search pilots from Oct 2026, gradual rollout from Jan 2027. DKI survey Feb 2026 (489 hospitals): 26% expected hospital-wide use in Q1 2026, 43% not before Q3. heise, 1 Oct 2026: still only few clinics fill the record.
findings.number: search beyond metadata: 2027 earliest; 43% of hospitals not before Q3 2026
findings.quote: Krankenhausentlassbrief zunächst als PDF/A, perspektivisch aber als MIO
findings.source: DKG, Umsetzungshinweise für die elektronische Patientenakte, prozessual-technischer Teil, Version 2.4
findings.talk_use: The newest national system repeats the document problem, so extracting data from text stays relevant for years.

findings.claim: A German GP described the ePA in October 2026 as a digital clothesline with sealed, dated envelopes.
findings.detail: Press report on an initiative that demands a restart of health digitalisation; one critical voice from an advocacy group. Same report: about 5.85 million active insured users, about 8% of 73 million records.
findings.quote: Ich bekomme eine digitale Wäscheleine, an der hängen mit Datum verschlossene Briefumschläge.
findings.source: heise online, Bündnis fordert: Gesundheit besser digitalisieren, 29 Oct 2026
findings.talk_use: A very good image for 'from documents to data'; attribute it as an opinion.

findings.claim: In a German survey on discharge management, 97% of hospital staff still sent discharge letters and documents by fax.
findings.detail: Innovation fund project KomK-K (hospital to insurer communication), reported by Ärzte Zeitung in Dec 2025. No sample size in the article; the original report was not read. The cabinet bill GeDIG (15 July 2026) plans to end fax in healthcare by autumn 2029 (trade press, it-boltwise).
findings.source: Ärzte Zeitung, Wenn die Klinik Faxe in die Praxis schickt, 11 Dec 2025
findings.talk_use: Light aside; say 'in one survey' and that it concerns discharge communication.

findings.claim: At a US trauma centre, 52% of transferred patients had a repeat CT within 24 hours, but only a minority because earlier images were unavailable.
findings.detail: 368 of 711 transfers, 2009 to 2017; in 41 patients earlier images were unavailable, mostly because the disc would not open (71%). Counter-evidence: a shared EHR in Massachusetts changed duplicate imaging from 29.4% to 20.7%, not significant (n=201, reports only, PMC7210344).
findings.number: 51.7% repeat CT; 41 patients with unavailable images
findings.source: Houston R et al., Cureus 2021;13(8):e17383
findings.talk_use: Use carefully: access alone does not remove repeat imaging. No German figure found.

findings.claim: Introducing a structured EHR in two Dutch university hospitals did not lengthen consultations but changed how the time was used.
findings.detail: 24 physicians, 439 consultations, observed before and after. Former legacy-EHR centre: dedicated patient care time fell by 8.5%. Former paper centre: dedicated documentation time rose by 8.3%.
findings.source: Joukes E et al., Appl Clin Inform 2018, doi:10.1055/s-0037-1615747
findings.talk_use: Answer to 'why not just fill in forms everywhere': the cost is paid at the point of care.

findings.claim: After a Norwegian university hospital moved to a structured EHR, free text remained the preferred method, and physicians distrusted some structured data because colleagues kept writing text.
findings.detail: Qualitative study, Sept 2023 to Jan 2024, observations and interviews, thematic analysis, one hospital. Related perspective paper: Rosenbloom 2011 (JAMIA, PMC3116264, full text) already proposed letting clinicians choose between structured entry and text with later processing.
findings.quote: free text remained the preferred method, with some exceptions
findings.source: Golburean O et al., JMIR Form Res 2025;9:e63902
findings.talk_use: Half-filled forms undermine trust; 'write freely, structure later' is an old idea that better text processing makes practical.

findings.claim: Structured radiology reporting does not always win: in a 2026 PSMA PET/CT study, free-text reports were rated higher for quality and for guiding decisions.
findings.detail: 50 patients, two readers. Information sufficient for treatment decision: 91% free text vs 76% structured; overall quality 5.46 vs 4.71. Structured reports were generated retrospectively by template. Other studies (for example dental panoramic images) found the opposite, so template design matters.
findings.source: Biechele G et al., Eur Radiol Exp 2026, doi:10.1186/s41747-026-00777-0
findings.talk_use: Radiology counter-example for Q&A on structured reporting.

caveats: The 3 hours per day figure is an estimate by hospitals (DKI) or self-report (Marburger Bund). Direct observation gives 93 min (19.4%) in one hospital and 20.5% writing in Leipzig. Definitions differ.
Text-versus-code overlap depends on NLP quality and thresholds, and both studies show structured data that is missing in text. Do not turn 13% into '87% unstructured'.
The Leipzig search time study used SAP i.s.h.med and COPRA, not ORBIS. No ORBIS-specific time or quality study was found here.
MD audits are selected, and about 60% concern length of stay or admission need. They are not a coding error rate. The Q2 2026 percentages are own sums from the official file.
The 6.57% abstraction error rate rests on papers from 1978 to 2008, mostly uncontrolled. With quality control 1.0 to 2.6% was reached.
Note bloat and record size evidence is from US health systems with other documentation incentives; transfer to Germany is an assumption.

The study on duplicate patient records and mortality (BMJ Qual Saf 2026, doi:10.1136/bmjqs-2025-019112) is observational, did not account for number of diagnoses or encounters, and was only read as press release. Not recommended as evidence of harm.

Quotes from web pages came through a fetch tool that uses a small model; quotes from the DKI, DKG and DigitalRadar reports were taken from the PDF text. Re-check quotes before printing them on a slide.
Moby Dick: the paper counts encounters (19.12%), press texts say patients.
Wright 2015, Tam 2005 and Smith 2005 (missing information in 13.6% of US primary care visits) are old and partly from paper times.
gaps: Hospital survey on ePA use after February 2026 (web search budget was exhausted).
German measurement of text duplication or record size in a hospital information system.
Survey or log data on number of IT systems or clicks per task in German hospitals.
German evidence on harm from missing information, duplicate imaging after transfer or missed findings.
Time spent on chart review by German doctoral candidates beyond the Erlangen cohort (2017).
Registry error rates for Germany (only a search snippet: Irish arthroplasty registry, about 9% form errors, PMC10995744, not read).
Fax and paper share in German hospitals with sample size; KomK-K report not read.
Originals of the 1998 Merrill Lynch / Coopers & Lybrand claim and Grimes 2008 (404) not read.
